entries.title: X Says Australia’s Under-16s Social Media Ban Risks Interfering With Foreign Law
entries.summary: Elon Musk's platform hit out at the country's “invasive” information-gathering powers as it demands the government drop efforts to strengthen its no-children policy.
entries.content:
X has a new argument against sweeping underage social media bans which would limit usage of its platform: They interfere with international law.

The social media platform, which sits within Elon Musk’s SpaceX, issued a submission to the Australian Parliament published Tuesday that called for the government to drop efforts to strengthen its underage social media ban. It complained that the proposals to increase pressure on sites to demonstrate efforts to crack down on underage access are unnecessary, ill-suited, unfair, and could violate privacy rights.

X pushed back against the “highly invasive” information gathering powers the proposed amendment would allow, accusing the commissioner of having “seemingly no understanding” of how this would work for the platforms and no safeguards for confidential and commercially sensitive information. Demanding data, documents, and compliance evidence from non-Australians in other countries could cause issues “for the comity of nations,” the firm also warned.

Australia is leading a growing global movement to restrict children’s access to social media, after banning under-16s from the sites in December. In May, the country ordered X to pay a $463,000 fine for failing to comply with child safety measures. The country’s internet regulator eSafety first issued the fine in 2023, claiming X did not respond sufficiently to a request for information on how it was tackling the spread of child sexual abuse content online, submitted one month before Elon Musk took over Twitter, now X.

X has previously criticized the country’s “excessive” penalty regime and complained in the most recent submission that a proposal to increase penalties against individuals is “entirely unjustified and disproportionate.”

Musk has been a particularly vocal critic of Australia’s bill to make 16 years the minimum age for social media. “Seems like a backdoor way to control access to the Internet by all Australians,” he wrote on X when the legislation was announced in late 2024. When Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez announced similar measures in February this year, Musk called him a “tyrant” and “true fascist totalitarian.”

While many digital rights campaigners believe the blanket age bans on social media are “problematic,” the information-gathering powers are not the issue, says Stefania Di Stefano, a researcher in international law and technologies.

“For me, the complete ban from social media on children and minors is problematic from an international human rights perspective,” says Di Stefano. “It is disproportionate with respect to the right of children to exercise their right to freedom of expression, their right to access information, their right to association, and so on and so forth.”

But Julia Hörnle, a professor of internet law at Queen Mary University of London, is skeptical about X’s submission. “A regulator in Australia ordering X to disclose a document in relation to their business activities in Australia, that’s perfectly fine,” she tells WIRED. “From all the data in the possession of the social media company, they can distinguish between Australian and non-Australian children, and therefore keep regulation to Australia.”

entries.title: Festival Must-Haves, Field-Tested at Lost Lands and Electric Forest
entries.summary: Our field-tested gear includes power banks, electrolytes, outdoor blankets, earplugs, and more.
entries.content:
The best festival gear, of course, depends on which festival you’re attending, the weather, your sleeping arrangements, and a ton of other factors. But as a longtime festival veteran, I’ve field-tested enough gear (and made enough mistakes) to have solid recommendations for preventing blisters, dehydration, a dead phone, and other common pitfalls in most situations. You'll find my top picks below.

Be sure to check out our other related buying guides, including the Best Tents, the Best Sleeping Bags, and the Best Bluetooth Speakers.

Updated July 2026: I've reformatted this guide with refreshed picks and a new look. I've also checked prices and accuracy throughout.

My Favorite Festival Gear

Best Electrolytes

These electrolytes are my favorite in general, and I especially like them for festivals because the ingredient concentrations are high enough that they actually help with efficient hydration when you're hot and sweaty. And the flavors are tasty, too, so I can pass them out to my crew and know they’ll actually drink them. Hydration is of utmost importance when it comes to preventing hangovers and “wook flu,” and this mixture can help. Plus, the packets don’t take up much space in your bag or pocket.

Best Outdoor Blanket

I have yet to try a blanket from Rumpl that I dislike. They pack up and unfurl easily, and most of them have enough space for seating multiple people. They also have little hooks to convert the blanket into a cape, which is nice if it gets chilly at camp but you aren’t ready to go to bed yet. They’re also easy to clean, whether they’re covered in dust or grass blades or spilled White Claw.

For just one or two people, this smaller blanket is perfect. It’s thin, so it’s best for summer or as an added layer.

My Favorite Power Bank

I’m not sure what it is about festivals that seems to make my phone die twice as fast, but it’s practically a law of the universe at this point. (It’s likely that the lack of cell service means my phone is constantly searching for a signal; read our tips on how to save battery life here.) Or maybe it's just overheating in my backpack. In any case, a power-bank phone charger with a large capacity is really handy. This Anker power bank isn’t the slimmest or the lightest, but it charges up quickly and can rapidly top off multiple devices per charge. Added bonus: You won’t be overpaying for the luxury of a charging locker. I bring two of these to four-day festivals and they keep my phone, speaker, Apple Watch, and other essentials charged the whole time. You might also want a MagSafe power bank around as a backup, though I prefer the efficiency of a larger brick.

A Dedicated Friend Finder

The Totem Compass was designed with festivals in mind. It uses satellites and its own proprietary mesh network to let you find your friends without any cell service or Wi-Fi. No more manually time-stamping your text messages or waving your phone around in the air trying to get a signal. Once these trackers are set up, you'll be able to navigate to your friend group with ease, just by looking down and walking toward their corresponding light color. Setup is a little tricky, and the battery life could be longer. You'll also need a way to charge them overnight for a multiday camping festival (the power bank I recommended above is an option). But they worked reliably for my pals and I to hunt each other down, and I felt safer going to stages by myself with another layer of security. And yes, they look cool while you're dancing, which certainly isn’t a detractor.

My Go-To Earplugs

The Loop Experience 2 are my favorite earplugs overall. They’re part of my daily carry, which is made easier by the convenient case. They protect your hearing without muffling the sound, and they look visually striking which also helps my friends know I’m wearing them so they don't attempt talking to me on the dance floor. I like how the case flips open, so I'm not jostling to unscrew a metal case in a crowd.

A Lighted Mirror

If you aren’t staying in a hotel (or if you are but your room is cramped), a lighted makeup mirror is invaluable for getting ready. I take the Fancii Abigail with me to every festival. Having a base station helps a lot with elaborate makeup looks or braided hairstyles, and the light is bright enough that you'll be able to see what you're doing, even if you're getting ready in a tent. It's large enough to give you the full picture, but small enough that it’ll fit in your backpack or duffel bag, even if you're a chronic overpacker like I am. Just make sure you're not breaking any rules about glass at the venue. I also like that it gives me a place to put all the random stickers I’m gifted.

A Camping Stove

There are a ton of great camp stoves, but this MSR stove is my favorite for festivals, because I’m not usually making full-size meals (though I have successfully used it to heat up a skillet and make an entire steak dinner). Often my site is just boiling water for pour-over coffee (speaking of coffee, we have a guide for rugged French presses right here) or warming up food we prepared at home. The PocketRocket 2 twists onto fuel canisters and heats up everything lightning-fast. When my group was stranded at a raceway in Ohio, we whipped this stove out and made coffee on top of our car trunk. It’s extremely compact and lightweight—so much so that my only gripe is that I have a hard time finding it between festival trips.

An Inflatable Couch

This inflatable couch is clutch if you don’t mind toting around a carrying case. These days, I keep my on-person carry pretty minimal, so I prefer to only use one if I have a wagon where I can chuck it when not in use. Fully inflated, it can support one to three people (provided everyone’s alright with getting cozy). When there's limited seating, or you’re on day three with two more days to go, an inflatable couch can provide respite with little effort. I also like that it comes in a ton of fun colors. Just make sure you’re aware of your surroundings—if you’re at a music festival, it’s bad manners to set up a couch in the middle of the crowd. Consider chilling back by the sound booths instead.

Pro tip: A folding hand fan makes inflation super easy if you don’t want to run around to fill the couch with air (yes, that’s really how you inflate it). It’s also cheaper to buy one of these ahead of time than from a vendor at the festival.

Sun Protection

This soft sun hat is easy to pack and bring along, since it folds up, but it still retains its shape to protect your head. It's a nice large size to keep your scalp, forehead, and neck protected without feeling too suffocating or providing too much coverage to be cute. It’s reversible, too; I like flipping between brown and beige depending on how sunny it is outside and which one matches my outfit better. —Nena Farrell

If you prefer lotion sunscreen, I like everything I’ve tried from Vacation, and this big jug is the perfect size to keep at camp. It contains enough product for me and my friends, and it absorbs quickly without feeling greasy or sticky.

More Festival Gear I Recommend

Fun, but Not Necessary

Kandi-making kits: Trading beaded bracelets is a hallmark of the electronic music scene, but thanks to the Taylor Swift Eras tour, fans of more music genres are joining in. Any beads will work, but I highly recommend Stretch Magic elastic—the cheap stuff falls apart way too easily.

Flow props: Some dancers like to use flow toys, as you’ll quickly see on the fringes of any festival crowd. I’m partial to the Fiberflies Pixel Whip, but the Flowtoys PodPoi are another popular choice. You can even get levitating wands and light-up staffs. These are super fun to dance with (and they’ll entertain your fellow attendees). Consider finding a Flow Jam in your area to try a few out before investing in your own.

Little gifts: Tiny ducks. Sprouts for your hair. Squishy animals. Festivals often have a culture of gift-giving. It’s not expected, but it can be nice to have something to pass out to the folks you meet. Consider bringing some trinkets with you—you might even make a new friend or seven. Even better if they're thrifted or repurposed.

Fun clothes: When it comes to festival clothing, you can be as bold or as practical as you’d like. Don’t sacrifice comfort in the name of fashion, but if you’re looking for fun clothes to wear, I recommend checking out IHeartRaves and Rave Wonderland. These are EDM-adjacent, but they’ll work for everything from Bonnaroo to Burning Man to EDC. Your favorite artists’ merch is probably a good starting point, too. And when in doubt, you can always accessorize—consider a bucket hat or a Pashmina-style shawl to make your outfit a little more adventurous.

How Does WIRED Test Festival Gear?

I test this gear at festivals by using it the same exact way you would. Speaker recommendations are tested with EDM Soundcloud mixes; earplugs are tested in front of Funktion Ones and Danley rigs; outdoor blankets are tested at silent discos and in dusty fields. I also solicit the opinions of my friends both old and new when testing gear. Most of the items in this guide have been tested at at least three fests.

Why I Know What I'm Talking About

I’ve been attending live music events since I was a teenager and have been to festivals all around the country, including heavy hitters such as Lost Lands and Electric Forest as well as smaller festivals that are still gatekept and require “roughing it.” I've experienced camping, car camping, glamping, and hotel and Airbnb stays. I haven't traveled internationally for a fest yet, but otherwise, I’ve probably experienced every situation you can think of, including severe weather and days-long security delays.

On Harm Reduction

Regardless of your personal habits, drug use can be prevalent at festivals. It's important to know the location of medical tents, pay attention to your surroundings, and look out for your fellow festival attendees the way you'd want them to look out for you.

I highly recommend getting trained in administering naloxone (Narcan). It prevents opioid overdose, and it’s cheap and easy to obtain along with training on how to use it. I took training through EndOverdose online. It took half an hour and cost $5. I liken it to knowing CPR or choking rescue; you hope you never have to use it, but it’s really good to have the knowledge just in case.

I also recommend looking into drug testing kits. You can obtain these from The Bunk Police and DanceSafe. Fentanyl testing strips are affordable, and it takes little time to test any substances that may be around. Some festivals have vendor tents that will test substances with amnesty. It doesn't hurt to be prepared.

Finally, I recommend signing up for alerts from BunkBot when applicable. It's an emergency alert system that texts folks if dangerous substances are found. It adds another layer of harm reduction and helps you be extra aware when needed.

entries.title: The 15 Best Pool Accessories to Upgrade Your Summer (2026)
entries.summary: These are the cleaning robots, water monitors, and toys actually worth buying for pool season.
entries.content:
Pools are hard. This is not news to anyone who owns one, but the uninitiated may not know about the inordinate amount of daily labor and chores that lie behind a pool’s clear, sparkling, perfectly chlorinated (or salted) water.

Luckily, pool tech has come a long way in the past decade—gone are the hours spent scooping leaves and dead bugs out of the water with a long-handled net, laboring over pH strips, and trying to relax on floaties too small for your adult-sized behind. We've now got robots that clean your pool, apps that monitor water quality from your phone, and even a slushie machine for proper pool-party margs.

With gas and plane ticket prices soaring to astronomical levels, there's never been a better time for a staycation at your own pool. (If you don't have a pool of your own, you can always rent one nearby on Swimply.) My colleague Christopher Null has a 12- by 36-foot, L-shaped, in-ground pool lined with PebbleTec, and I have a 20- by 12-foot above-ground pool lined with vinyl. Between the two of us, we have pretty much tried it all, so whether you've got a custom-built in-ground complex or an Intex pop-up from Walmart, these time- and life-tested swimming pool accessories are sure to level up your backyard pool game.

For more yard-tech tips, check out our guides to the Best Pool Cleaning Robots, Best Smart Sprinklers and Irrigation Systems, Best Robot Lawn Mowers, and Best Smart Bird Feeders.

Updated July 2026: I’ve added a sun hat, a wave machine, a pool thermometer, a whimsical speaker, and a water bottle. I also ensured up-to-date links and prices. Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

  • Instant Lap Pool
  • The Best Pool Alarm
  • For Keeping an Eye on Things
  • Stop Skimming Leaves
  • Outsource Your Water-Quality Chores
  • Critical Sun Protection
  • Is It Warm Enough to Go In?
  • For Floating Around With a Drink
  • Never Vacuum Again
  • A More Affordable Robot
  • A Water Bottle You Won’t Lose
  • The Best Resort Towels
  • For Peak Margarita Szn
  • Sunglasses That Float
  • A Speaker With Vibes

Instant Lap Pool

What, you’re still swimming in a still-water pool? Get with the ’20s and add an artificial wave machine that uses jets of water to create a strong current that you can swim against.

iGarden’s Swim Jet X (also available in a few cheaper, lower-power versions) is a massive pump that clips onto the edge of your pool deck, cycling up to 1,100 gallons of water per minute through its 31-pound chassis, creating its powerful stream. At higher settings, this current is downright extreme, able to blast an unprepared swimmer halfway across the pool. The result is a very effective way to exercise without swimming long laps in a traditional lap pool. And if the kids just want to splash around a bit for fun, you can lower the Swim Jet’s intensity level to create a lighter, surface-level disturbance.

The Swim Jet isn’t perfect, though. The workouts are challenging and also adjustable, thanks to the machine’s six power modes. Even so, swimming in place may not provide quite as vigorous an exercise session as traditional laps. Battery life is another consideration: You’ll get 10 hours of running time on the slowest, lowest setting, but its efficiency plummets as you ratchet up the output. On the higher power modes, the system is good for about two hours of wave-blasting operation.

It’s also very expensive, with the top-tier version running $4,320 at some sellers. That’s astronomical in price, but what pool product isn’t? And compared to the cost of a membership at a gym that has a pool, it might make more sense than it seems.

The Best Pool Alarm

If you (or your neighbors) have small children, investing in a pool alarm may very well be an invaluable insurance policy. Lifebuoy’s Bcone is the blue-chip alarm option on the market right now. It’s a bright red, double-ended cone that floats in your pool (or hot tub) and sounds a siren if something ends up in the water that isn’t supposed to be there.

The system works by detecting disturbances to the water’s surface, analyzing wave patterns to distinguish between the splash of a person (or pet) falling in and ripples caused by the wind. If the Bcone detects an event, it fires off its internal Klaxon and relays the alarm to a Wi-Fi bridge that remains inside the home (plus the Bcone app). The bridge and app both let you easily disable the alarm when people are swimming—and can even turn the system back on automatically when the water is clear, so “I forgot” doesn’t become a deadly excuse. —Christopher Null

For Keeping an Eye on Things

This is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill's pick for best outdoor security camera after testing many models. Though I personally have an older Arlo model, I agree that the brand makes the most consistently user-friendly security cameras on the market right now. Recorded footage of your pool is another important investment in safety and potential liability, especially if you have children or curious animals living nearby. A camera can also function as a tool to help proactively spot potential issues while you're away from home, such as the water level, cleaning-equipment functionality, and cover positioning.

Stop Skimming Leaves

As someone who manually fished leaves and dead bees out of their pool with a net for years, I can attest to the utility of an automatic skimmer. It's not cheap, but if you have a large pool that doesn't have an in-wall skimming system, a robotic skimmer is a must-have, and this is the pool-cleaning robot reviewer Christopher Null likes best. It's solar-powered, so you never have to take it out to charge, and it's got sensors that help it avoid damaging itself by running into your pool walls. Read the full rundown in our guide to the Best Pool Cleaning Robots.

Outsource Your Water-Quality Chores

Cleaning out debris is only one part of regular pool maintenance. Equally important, if not more so, is keeping chemicals in balance. If things get out of whack for even a few days, you can be left with a green, algae-ridden mess that is a major challenge to remedy. Test strips and kits have long been standard, but they're a hassle to use and only give you a snapshot of your pool’s chemistry at a specific moment in time. Smart technology offers a much more elegant solution; it lets you keep tabs on chemistry in real time and alerts you if something’s amiss. Of the handful of smart-pool chemistry monitors I’ve tested, I like Iopool’s Eco Start the best.

This floating gadget monitors temperature, pH, and ORP (a stand-in for free chlorine), together giving you a solid picture of your pool’s disinfection capabilities. It automatically updates every 15 minutes. While many chemistry monitors require replaceable supplies (which is a costly approach) and regular battery replacements to work, Iopool’s solution is solid-state, needing no maintenance at all except for storing it out of the pool in winter months. I used mine for two full swimming seasons until it died (at which point it must be replaced)—and I like it so much I just dropped its successor into the water for the summer. —Christopher Null

Critical Sun Protection

Notice you tend to burn faster when you’re in the pool than hiking or performing activities on land? It’s not your imagination—water acts as a mirror, reflecting a portion of the sun’s UV rays. This means every time you’re in the water or even just hanging out nearby, your UV exposure is compounded from both direct sunlight and the water around you. A wide-brimmed hat can help protect a larger skin surface area, and this one from Solbari sports UPF 50+ nylon-and-cotton fabric as well as a brim that’s larger than typical hats of this style—5 inches in the front and 6 in the back. I tested this hat in the pool on days pushing 100 degrees Fahrenheit, and not only did I not get burned, but I also found the hat itself didn’t feel very hot, especially if I flipped the color side (it comes in navy, pink, ice blue, or green) to the cream side.

Is It Warm Enough to Go In?

My above-ground pool has a wimpy solar-exchange heater, so a pool thermometer is critical for knowing if the water is, in fact, warm enough to swim in. These TempPro models have been reliable in my tests, and I like that there's a separate display with a magnet on the back, so you don't need to use an app or even bother with a phone at all. The solar model stays charged and can transmit the temperature from about 150 feet away to my house and through its walls. (The range is supposedly 500 feet.) Note that I compared the TempPro temperature readings with those of a pricier pool thermometer and a probe thermometer—the actual temperature consistently ran a few degrees cooler than all of those readings. But this was easy to keep in mind.

For Floating Around With a Drink

When our first 90-degree-Fahrenheit day popped up on the forecast last month, I immediately started searching for an affordable floating cooler for drinks with a sun-blocking canopy, and I ended up buying this Funboy model off Amazon. It can easily handle a six-pack of cans on a raft of ice, the canopy is removable, and there's a drink holder on either side so you and your buddy can push it back and forth between your floats. The striped design with the fringe is very St. Tropez (or ’80s-era pool umbrella, depending on your age and station), and I ended up liking the vibe so much that I have since added its companion matching inflatable pool float rings, which come in 16 colors on Funboy's site or six on Amazon. I've had the rings in my pool for over a month now, in direct sun, and while I wish they had handles for easier on-and-off movement, they have held up great. The 48-inch size is big enough for most adult butts, and also comes with the requisite cupholder. However, note that the cupholder design is very small and very shallow, so you may want to stick with the more forgiving holders on the cabana bar.

Never Vacuum Again

Manual pool vacuums are so last century. WIRED reviewer Christopher Null has been testing pool-cleaning robots for four years, and this one from Beatbot, he says, is the best he's tried. It not only excels at its prescribed cleaning tasks, but its battery charge is also phenomenal at six hours, it has AI-powered debris detection, and its companion app is great. It can also skim your pool's surface if needed. Best of all, it floats when it's done, so you don't have to retrieve it from the bottom of the pool. (Which is good, he says, because it's quite heavy.)

A More Affordable Robot

If your pool-robot budget is more pool noodle than Portofino, you may want to take a look at Beatbot's Sora 30. WIRED reviewer Christopher Null found it had outstanding performance for the price and excellent battery life, and, just like its pricier sibling above, floats when it's done. It doesn't have a whole lot of smart features, but you'll still have the option of multiple modes through Beatbot's app.

A Water Bottle You Won’t Lose

I always have a water bottle at the pool, but it often doesn't stay cold all day, hold enough liquid, or stand out enough for me to avoid forgetting it when I leave. This one from Dometic, though, hits all three notes. I filled it with ice and water and left the bottle in direct sun during a stretch of 80-degree-Fahrenheit temperatures, and the water stayed cold for three days. You can add your preferred lid and collar (the strap collar shown comes standard, and the sip lid is an extra $15), or go with the standard flip-up lid. I like the yellow for visibility—and to match the brand's excellent Recon coolers, which I'm always hauling somewhere—but it comes in six other colors if that's not your thing.

The Best Resort Towels

Any respectable pool day begins and ends with a quality towel, and Cozy Earth’s are the best I’ve ever tried. My favorite from the brand’s lineup is the Seaside Resort Towel. Made from OEKO-TEX–certified 100 percent cotton, it’s perfectly thick and plush and large enough to drape over a chaise. It will lose some fluffiness after about three washes, but most towels do. The Classic Stripe Resort Towel is also solid but slightly less plush, with a cotton-viscose blend but more color options (six, compared with the Seaside's two). One side also has a low pile, which works well for the beach, as it will trap less sand.

For Peak Margarita Szn

You haven't properly pool-partied until you've languished on your pool float on a hot day with a frozen margarita in hand. Or a cup of frosé, frozen lemonade, or just about anything else you can think of—it will probably slush in one of our favorite slushie machines. High-sugar drinks work best, but you can even slush diet drinks by adding allulose. If you want to keep two drinks going at a time, Ninja has you covered with its just-released dual-reservoir version, which WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage crowned as the best for parties. It can auto-adjust temperatures to ensure drinks with different consistencies are ready at the same time.

Sunglasses That Float

Drop your sunglasses in the pool? (Or lake? Or river? Or ocean?) Typically, that's the last you'll see of that pair. But not now! These lightweight, inexpensive frames from no-slip, no-bounce sunglasses giant Goodr will float, so you can easily grab them next time you pass them on your inflatable lounge. They come in five colors (including Seafoam Party Favor, shown) and are great for all kinds of athletic pursuits, from running to paddleboarding and beyond.

A Speaker With Vibes

These Bluetooth speakers are designed to look like tiki torches, with a faux flickering amber flame. You can screw them onto yard stakes (not included), or just set them right next to the pool for ambient effect. They’re cute, festive, and more fun than a typical Bluetooth speaker, but note that they are slightly tinny, novelty-quality speakers, so don’t expect to be bumping any kind of bass. You’ll also likely need two for surround sound. (I have only one, which did not do a great job with multichannel recordings.) Still, one or two make a fun gift or an addition to a summer-themed gift basket.

entries.title: Love It or Hate It, the Ferrari Luce Is a Thrilling Drive
entries.summary: WIRED test-drove a preproduction version of the Luce, the storied Italian automaker’s controversial electric car, and it was remarkably surprising. Will it convert Ferrari fanatics?
entries.content:
Some still believe that you can’t manage a car company unless you’re a fully paid-up “car guy.” Tell that to Benedetto Vigna, Ferrari’s CEO. He’s a physicist by education, hired to run the company in 2021 after a career in semiconductors, although he did significant business with automotive during that time.

Vigna also helped develop a three-dimensional motion sensor first used in airbags, later adapted for the Nintendo Wii and the iPhone’s screen rotation function. An inventor, then. “I prefer innovator,” he once told me. “A lot of the time inventors are just thinking, but innovators conceive new things and make them happen.”

This is all useful background to the Luce, Ferrari’s first fully electric car, engineered in Maranello, Italy, but designed in California by LoveFrom, the agency set up by renowned iPhone designer Jony Ive. It’s not Apple’s abandoned car, reskinned and rebooted for the world’s most famous automotive name, but more the product of a union between like-minded innovators—Italian spirit and attitude, Silicon Valley lateral thinking.

But unless you’ve been hiding under a rock on Mars with Elon Musk these past few months, you’ll also know that the result didn’t land the way its creators would have anticipated. Ferrari’s immense global fan base is seemingly not on board with the idea of an electric car on a point of principle. And hiring Ive and his team to reimagine the aesthetic has proven as welcome as Kryptonite is to Superman.

Part of the frequently obnoxious discourse around the Luce centered around the idea that a Ferrari’s design should deliver an instant dopamine rush. These aren’t cars that require a PhD in design to understand; they’re meant to hit hard and fast, seeding desire the moment you see them. The Luce spectacularly breaks from tradition, and without the famous Prancing Horse badge, there’s little here that yokes it to perhaps the most revered automotive back catalog of all. But that was all part of the brief: Do something different.

The driving experience amplifies this feeling. The Luce is a Ferrari, just not the sort we’re used to. “In the past 100 years, technology has changed for sure,” Raffaele de Simone, Ferrari’s chief test driver, tells me. “But what hasn’t changed is our bodies. We have two hands, two eyes and ears, and two feet. The interface is the same—steering, brakes and throttle—but the Luce has a different sort of driving emotion and a different way of announcing driving thrills.”

Driving Different

I was at a test track in northern Italy in May to find out how successfully that’s been achieved. I was in a preproduction car, still disguised at the time of driving because it pre-dates the car’s reveal in Rome. First impressions? The Luce’s cab-forward proportions mean you sit closer to the front axle than usual, and higher because there’s a large battery pack beneath the cabin. It’s clearly not low-slung or sporty.

You can’t help but take in that interior, clearly Apple-inspired but positing a whole new approach to territory that has seen an entire generation of new cars lose sight of first principles. The three-spoke wheel’s design is inspired by a classic Ferrari’s, and it feels fantastic. The air vents pivot with a deeply engineered precision. Even the seat runners are elegant. The space in the rear is almost limo-like.

One of Ive’s superpowers is being able to detect the level of care invested in a product's design, and whether you like the Luce’s aesthetic or not, that’s indisputable. But he rejects the concept of a touchscreen inside a car, choosing instead to elevate haptic feel and the clarity of the dials to a level previously unseen in the automotive context. Ive is all about input and output. The Luce is a special place to be.

There’s a slickness to the first driving impressions, too. Ferraris have become less highly strung over the years, with greater emphasis now placed on daily usability. As befits its four-door, five-seat layout, the Luce is arguably the most accessible Ferrari in the company’s near-80-year history. Its major controls—the throttle and brake pedal—are beautifully calibrated, so it moves away effortlessly with an impressively and perhaps unexpectedly light touch. On some classic Ferraris, you have to let the gearbox oil warm thoroughly before going anywhere. This is not an issue on the Luce, despite its complex electronic drive units.

The structure is all new. The chassis consists of hollow castings, extrusions and aluminum sheets, to reduce weight and optimize load paths. The 800-volt battery architecture is integrated into the chassis, positioned as low in the Luce’s floorpan as the engineers could achieve. So it has a center of gravity that’s 95 mm lower than the Purosangue, Ferrari’s quasi-SUV, and a yaw moment of inertia 15 percent less than that car. That means it’s more agile and changes direction more keenly.

That’s physics in play. Ferrari’s commitment to technology is greater than ever, and the Luce deploys everything it knows to manage those external forces. It enjoys unprecedented control of each wheel in all three axes (lateral, longitudinal, and vertical), with particular emphasis on lateral body dynamics. A new “vehicle control unit” oversees power delivery and energy recovery, and updates target metrics 200 times per second. As with all high-end electric vehicles, the Luce’s master controller has a lot to do.

Prancing Power

The electric Ferrari has a 122-kWh battery and four e-motors, two on each axle, and optimum weight distribution. The front motors deliver 282 brake horsepower (bhp), the rears 831 bhp, so the total output is north of 1,000 bhp. And there’s mammoth torque: 5,900 pound-feet (around 8,000 Newton-meters) at the rear wheels, a crazy amount of force.

The front motors can spin at up to 30,000 revolutions per minute and can go from nothing to maximum in less than a second. The chassis and body consist of 75 percent recycled aluminum. There’s also a separate rear subframe for the first time on a Ferrari; it’s connected to the rest of the chassis by elastomeric bushes—polymers with a high viscosity—which helps reduce noise and vibration.

A new “e-manettino” dial on the lower left of the steering wheel joins the existing one on the right, a staple of all Ferraris since its arrival in 2004’s F430 model. The new addition has three settings that govern power and traction, as well as the shape of the torque curve. In Range mode, power is limited to 429 bhp, and the car is predominantly rear-drive. Select Tour, and the driver has 608 bhp to enjoy, with all-wheel drive capability. In the Performance setting, that rises to 958 bhp, and the top speed is raised to a maximum of 190 mph.

Engineering this sort of bandwidth into an EV is nothing new. However, the application here is more emotionally charged: Ferrari has an obligation to organize the possibilities as entertainingly as possible. How else will it be able to silence that fan base seemingly intent on shunning the concept of an electric Ferrari?

“What excites me is that we have more tools available than ever before to give the driver exactly what they’re asking from the car,” de Simone tells me. “Let’s say you’re entering a corner and suddenly the radius tightens. Instantly the driver is asking the car for a little more rotation. In that moment, rear-wheel steering, active suspension, and torque vectoring from the four motors are all working together to help achieve that response. What’s interesting is that you don’t necessarily feel the individual systems at work. What you feel is confidence.”

Because it can vector torque on both axles, the Luce’s dynamic behavior plays out in hi-def widescreen. The front end is positive without being overly sensitive; it remains neutral throughout the middle phase of the corner and has incredible traction on the exit. Ferrari long ago mastered the chassis hardware, but it's a software leader now, too; its Side Slip Control system reaches v10 in the Luce, and its traction control has evolved to suit the car’s quad-motor configuration. Select Performance mode and switch the other manettino to “CT off” (traction control off), and the Luce gets distinctly more playful. It’s doubtful that many owners will ever drift their $600,000 electric Ferrari, but it can certainly do it.

Like all engineers, Ferrari’s people love graphs and charts and will happily share what they deem is proof that the 4,982-pound Luce feels significantly less than that. Subjectively, it has the alertness and willingness to change direction of a much lighter car, but given that it’s five meters long and two meters wide, you still need space to explore these limits.

Electric Shifts, Kraftwerk Sounds

Further interactivity (and graphs) arrive in the form of the Luce’s Torque Shift Engagement. This is Ferrari’s answer to one of the issues with EVs: the rather one-dimensional way that they deliver their energy. Pull the right paddle on the steering column and you get five power and torque levels; the left one delivers five grades of regenerative engine braking, with incremental illumination within the instrument display so you can keep track of the deployment.

The Luce plays with the torque curve so that you feel like you’re fully in command during cornering entry and exit rather than simply riding a huge wave of torque. In essence, it’s designed to conjure the sensation you feel driving a car with a conventional transmission and engine braking. The amount of energy corresponds with the available grip and the nature of the corner itself. It’s a step up from the synthesized gearbox in the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N and the e-shift option available in the latest Porsche Taycan, as good as they are.

The Luce’s dynamic bandwidth extends to its ride quality, even on 23- and 24-inch wheels, and on the gnarliest surfaces. It’s fitted with the third generation of Ferrari’s 48-volt active suspension and controls its mass very adroitly without ever becoming floaty.

Finally, there’s the way it sounds. Largely silent, barring some mild wind and tire noise, the Luce finds its voice in Performance mode. There’s something of the harmonic rasp of a six-cylinder to it, and it’s not quite as rumbly as a V-8, never mind a V-12. But it’s real and musical—more Kraftwerk-adjacent than Pavarotti, perhaps—and has been achieved by using an accelerometer and by equalizing naturally occurring frequencies on the rear inverter.

“You can think about it like a musical instrument. It has its own timbre,” says Antonio Palermo, who led this part of the Luce’s development team. “We need to take away the annoying noise, because there’s no point amplifying gear whine, for example. But there are lots of other beautiful frequencies we can work with and let out. We talk about orchestras when it comes to ICE. Well, there’s a different type of orchestra inside this machine, too.”

The Luce clearly repositions and reimagines the very idea of what a Ferrari could be. For most people, that’s a romantic notion likely steeped in dreams of Italy at its most seductive, or a wailing combustion engine closing in on an 8,500-rpm redline. Hence the fallout. The Luce is on a different path, and it demands an alternative response. But in terms of how it drives, there’s no question it’s authentically Ferrari. We can’t wait to drive it again.

entries.title: 23 WIRED-Approved Gifts for Frequent Travelers (2026)
entries.summary: For the frequent flier who treats the Delta Sky Club like their second home.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

Gifts for travelers should focus on ease and peace of mind. Even the most seasoned globetrotter can find traveling stressful. Between packing, navigating overcrowded terminals, and living out of a suitcase, it can be overwhelming. Most jet-setters have their travel routine down to a science, but the perfect gift can enhance any experience, whether it's a three-day business retreat or a two-week adventure across Europe.

We’ve put together a list of essentials and luxurious gifts for travelers, from noise-canceling headphones to a weekend bag that carries it all. Be sure to check out our other gift guides as well, including the Best Gifts for Women, Gifts for Coworkers, and Best Stocking Stuffers.

Updated July 2026: I've added the Solbari Resort Wide Brim Sun Hat and removed discontinued products. Prices and links were also updated.

  • A Trackable Carry-On

    July

    Trackable Carry-On With CaseSafe

    July's latest suitcase has CaseSafe, built-in technology that is a

    Bluetooth trackerthat works with both Android Find Hub and iOS Find My. Simply open the suitcase, locate the tracker, pull the tab, and pair it with the respective app. There's also an ejectable USB-C rechargeablepower bankbeneath the handle. You can easily smarten up an old suitcase by adding an AirTag and a power bank, but having them built in means you cannot lose the tracker in a stray sock, and I like that the battery is accessible, so you can pop it out in case you need to gate-check your bag.

    In every other respect, July makes suitcases that many WIRED staffers have been happy with. I particularly like the wide range of heights on the handle and the distinctive, protective bumpers—my own two kids have played Bumper Suitcase while riding on July luggage at boring moments in the terminal, and they are still undamaged. It's worth noting that the carry-on is slightly too wide to meet some domestic airlines' size specifications, so check your favorite airline before you buy any suitcase. —Adrienne So

  • A Sun Hat

    Solbari

    Resort Wide Brim Sun Hat

    If you know a frequent traveler who’s always headed somewhere sunny and comes back with a sunburn to match, this UPF 50+ hat can keep their face and scalp safe from the sun’s bright rays. Solbari’s hats are all designed as sun protection with Ultraviolet Protection Factor built in. As a San Diego resident, I especially like this cute hat to keep my scalp from getting sunburned, but it would work well in any sunny setting. It travels well, too, since it’s soft and flexible. I throw it into the bottom of my beach bag or stroller for my outings, and it would be plenty easy to add to a carry-on without taking up much space at all. —

    Nena Farrell

  • Compression Packing Cubes

    Eagle Creek

    Pack-It Reveal Carry-On Set

    Frequent travelers who don't use collapsible cubes when packing are struggling, and they don't even know it. Give them this travel tip: Eagle Creek's set is

    the best, made of durable fabric with high-quality zipper pulls. EditorKat Mercksays there's just enough mesh for air circulation to prevent odor buildup or fabric degradation, and the bottom and back of the cubes are opaque for privacy. They're water-resistant and designed with a top handle. The largest cube in this set is also split into two sections for clean clothes and dirty laundry. Eagle Creek sells setsfor extended staysor slim shapes.

  • A Portable Hair Dryer

    Dyson

    Supersonic r Hair Dryer

    If precision, speed, and a lightweight build are all important to your frequent traveler, the Dyson Supersonic r is at the top of the market. It weighs just 0.7 pounds, which is 30 percent smaller and 20 percent lighter than other Dyson dryers—a game changer when every pound counts. It comes with five RFID-enabled attachments that auto-adjust heat and airflow to your last-saved preferences. Read my full

    review here.

  • A Travel Steamer

    Jack & Rose

    Travel Steamer

    For years, I thought I could avoid ever having to iron anything by only wearing clothes that don't wrinkle. This is an impossible ask, and everything wrinkles when you travel, so I finally caved and bought this travel steamer. It has a 100- to 200-volt range, so you can use it overseas. It's incredibly compact, heats up quickly, and is easy to use. The brand notes that its wrinkle-releasing capabilities are not comparable to a full-size steamer, but I found that even on the lowest setting, it removed wrinkles in one or two passes from my son's and husband's dress shirts on a recent trip. It's also slim and attractive on your bathroom counter. —Adrienne So

  • Travel Size Toiletries

    Ries

    The Essential Refillable Travel Container Set

    These Ries refillable bottles already come in a gift box, so half the job is already done for you. I love the rich pine green, which is festive for the holidays but still timeless enough for year-round use. Five airless pump bottles—three for your essentials (shampoo, conditioner, and body wash) and two for skin care (face wash and a blank bottle to go rogue). They're all TSA-approved: Each bottle is 3.4 ounces, except the face wash bottle, which is 1.7 ounces.

  • Universal Power

    Ceptics

    World International Travel Plug Adapter

    No one wants to be scrambling for an adapter during a layover or post-flight. When it comes to international

    travel adapters, the Ceptics World model is compatible with most regions (EU, UK, US, Australia, and China), so you’re covered almost anywhere you land. It also has three USB-A ports and two USB-C ports, so you can charge multiple gadgets at once. Your phone, laptop, tablet, and so forth will thank you.

  • Travel Books, Anytime

    Amazon

    Kindle Paperwhite (2024, 12th Generation)

    The

    Kindle Paperwhiteis the obvious gift for your bookworm friend. ReviewerNena Farrellsaysthe 12th-generation model has the highest contrast ratio on any Kindle and lasts up to three months on a charge. Its 7-inch display is crisp and easy on the eyes with its warm backlighting, whether it be in direct sun or a dim plane cabin. Plus, it’s water-resistant enough for poolside reading. The Signature Edition adds wireless charging, auto-brightness, and double the storage at 32 gigabytes.

  • Never Lose Baggage

    Apple

    AirTags (4-pack)

    Airports are chaotic enough without worrying about losing your luggage. I know

    AirTags can be a bit divisive, but they’re the best way to keep tabs on your valuables if you have an iPhone. Set up with the Find My app, and you'll always know where your bags are—even when the airline doesn't. Plus, with busy flights often leading to last-minute gate checks and delays, AirTags are well worth the extra security.

    If your loved one is an

    Androiduser, we recommend theChipolo One Point. OurBest Trackersguide also has more options.

  • MagSafe Travel Wallet

    Case-Mate

    Soap Bubble Magnetic Wallet for iPhone

    This is former reviewer

    Brenda Stolyar’s favorite MagSafe wallet. It’s by far one of the roomiest she’s tested, with enough space for five credit cards, cash, and some change. It’s sealed with a snap closure, so it’s chunkier than someother MagSafe wallets, but that extra space is a blessing when you’re carrying multiple currencies.

  • Hands-Free Explorer

    Got Bag

    Moonbag Small

    Every tourist needs a sidekick, and this GOT sling bag fits the bill. Wear it over the shoulder, as a crossbody bag, or around the waist. It’s roomy enough for all your travel gear: a phone, a wallet, a compact point-and-shoot camera, and a few other small essentials. I also love that it’s mainly made from recycled

    Ocean Impact Plastic.

  • Silence That Travels

    Bose

    QuietComfort Ultra Headphones

    Long flights can be a brutal test of endurance, but with Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones, they don’t have to be.

    Bose remains our top choicefor high-quality noise cancellation, cutting through the chaos, including that crying baby in 22B. With up to 18 hours of battery in Immersive Audio mode (or 24 without), they’ll last through the long hauls.

    If you’re after something more budget-friendly, check out our

    Best Noise-Canceling Headphonesguide,Best Wireless Headphonesguide, or consider theQuietComfort Ultra Earbudsfor Bose’s noise-canceling magic at almost half the price.

  • All-in-One Charger

    Anker

    MagGo 3-in-1 Charging Station (Qi2)

    This portable 3-in-1 charger is a great gift for on-the-go Apple lovers. It delivers up to 15 watts to an iPhone or Qi2-certified device via an adjustable magnetic pad, so you can doomscroll while you charge. There's a second pad tucked behind for AirPods (or other wireless earbuds) and a fold-out Apple Watch charger. Anker even includes a 5-foot USB-C cable and a wall adapter, all backed by a two-year warranty. Read our

    Best Apple 3-in-1 Wireless ChargersandBest Portable Chargersguides for other recommendations.

  • Airplane Audio Upgrade

    Twelve South

    Airfly Pro 2

    Airplanes are still living in the wired age, but thanks to the AirFly Pro 2, I can watch all the Big Bang Theory reruns I want in cordless bliss. Twelve South recently upgraded one of the most helpful accessories it offers. Just plug it into the seat-back jack, pair it with your wireless headphones (or earphones) via Bluetooth, et voilà!—you’re set for in-flight entertainment sans the questionable airline earbuds.

    The AirFly Pro 2 connects to most 3.5-mm audio jacks, from treadmills to gaming devices, so it’s a thoughtful gift idea for anyone who wants to stay connected on the go. The newer version has some great upgrades, like physical volume buttons and an updated Qualcomm chip for better sound, but you can still get

    the older versionfor about $20 less.

  • Comfort in Coach

    Trtl

    Neck Pillow

    The Trtl Neck Pillow is the ideal red-eye or road trip companion. Instead of constricting your neck in a doughnut, these scarf-style travel pillows have an internal frame that cradles your head without physical strain. It's lightweight—just half a pound—and packable; you can stuff it into its accompanying storage bag and clip it onto your travel bag when not in use.

  • Morning Brew

    AeroPress

    Clear

    For the camper or caffeinated wanderer in your life, the AeroPress Clear guarantees a robust cup of coffee in the morning, an afternoon pick-me-up, or an evening espresso (no judgment here). WIRED contributor

    Joe Rayswears thatit brews coffeejust as well as the Original AeroPress or the Go model. It’s also easy to clean, and with six additional colors, it adds a splash of personality if you have a somewhat blah-looking coffee setup.

  • Flight Relief

    Bombas

    Men's Everyday Compression Sock 3-Pack (15-20mmHg)

    When you’re traveling, your legs deserve a little TLC, and Bombas is just that. Available in men’s and women’s, these medium-compression socks (15-20 mmHg) boost circulation, reduce swelling, and help speed recovery after long days of travel and sightseeing. Bombas also gives back with every purchase, donating a pair of socks to someone in need.

  • Organized Tech

    Moment

    Everything Tech Organizer

    For the individual who’s always losing chargers (guilty), the padded Moment Tech Organizer almost makes it impossible to be disorganized. With six elastic cable holders and multiple compartments, this is the best gift for the digital nomad or a creative wanderer. It even has a “junk drawer” for power banks and other miscellaneous travel items. Moment also offers a mini version that I carry in my everyday tote bag.

  • Minty-Fresh Hygiene

    Moon Oral Beauty

    The Electric Toothbrush

    Reviewer

    Nena Farrellloves thiselectric toothbrushfor travel. It comes with a carrying case and extra brush heads for when you’re scrambling for spares mid-trip. Equipped with five cleaning modes, it's versatile enough for any giftee, and its slim charger fits easily into most toiletry bags. You can't go wrong with black, but the toothbrush is also available in gold, a Hello Kitty theme, and a Barbie edition.

  • KN95 Masks

    evolvetogether

    5 black KN95 masks (Rio de Janeiro)

    In our post-pandemic world, I can't imagine stepping foot into an airport without a

    face mask. KN95s may not be the most thrilling gift, but this five-pack from evolvetogether has a luxe factor that most would appreciate. They’re six-ply (with a water-resistant exterior), made with activated charcoal to reduce odors, and they’re hypoallergenic—so your giftee won’t have to worry about skin care when nerves are already at their peak.

  • Music That Travels

    JBL

    Clip 5

    There are moments when you just need

    a portable speaker(instead of earbuds or headphones)—like when you're jamming with friends, singing in the shower, or lounging at the beach. Reviewer Ryan Waniata describes the JBL Clip 5 speaker as having a warm sound, with fuller bass and midrange frequencies. You can clip it onto yourself (with its included carabiner) while sightseeing or cycling through a new city. It's also dust- and water-resistant, so it's safe to use in the shower.

  • Sleep Through Jet Lag

    Bearaby

    Tencel Sleep Mask

    Traveling means sacrificing the comfort of your bed and sometimes facing unpredictable sleeping conditions.

    A sleep eye maskis a small luxury that makes even the least ideal sleep arrangements more tolerable. I love Bearaby's full temple-to-temple coverage and gentle fit—it doesn't squeeze your head like some of the ones that airlines hand out. Made from natural eucalyptus fibers, it's breathable and anti-frizz, perfect if you're someone who styles their hair before flights.

  • Weekender for Every Trip

    Lo & Sons

    The OG 2

    A larger version of

    Lo & Sons' Nouvelle purse, the OG 2 is ready for anything—work commutes, overnights, full-day excursions—with a place for just about every essential. It has an exterior laptop sleeve for quick access at TSA (bless), a side compartment for shoes, and interior pockets for the rest of your travel accessories (including a slot for your emotional support water bottle). This is former WIRED editor Adrienne So’s go-to personal item for weekend trips; it's smaller than a duffel, fits under a flight seat, and is designed with a trolley sleeve to secure onto a suitcase. entries.title: Mac Mini Availability: Long Waits and Higher Prices
entries.summary: Thanks to the surge in local AI processing and the ongoing memory shortage, it’s incredibly difficult to buy a Mac Mini.
entries.content:
Three months ago, outgoing Apple CEO Tim Cook admitted that the company had been caught off guard by the sharp increase in demand for the Mac Mini. Cook said it may take “several months” to catch up with demand, fueled by a boom in people using the compact computer for local AI workloads.

Now, while the situation has improved slightly, things are far from normal. At its worst, the base configuration of the Mac Mini was completely sold out on Apple’s storefront. This is true at third-party retailers like Amazon or Best Buy. Apple has them back in stock for a while now on Apple.com, but slow shipping times still show how dire the situation is.

Longer Waits

When buying directly from Apple, the cheapest Mac Mini with only 16 GB of RAM ships in three to four weeks. A MacBook Air from Apple with the same 16 GB of RAM configuration has a delivery window of two to three weeks—same as the MacBook Neo with 8 GB of RAM.

RAM is the primary contributing factor to the delays, as the waits get longer as capacity increases. Mac Mini configurations with 36 GB of RAM have wait times of around a month, while 48 GB of memory will take three months or longer to ship to customers. Meanwhile, a Mac Studio with 48 GB of memory takes an estimated “13 to 14 weeks” to arrive. That's an incredibly long time to wait. These higher-end memory configurations aren't even on offer at Amazon or Best Buy.

The wait times may put Apple in conflict with its next update of the Mac Mini and Mac Studio. Apple has not updated the Mac Mini since October 2024, but rumors have been pointing to an M5 chip update this fall. That means if you order an M4 Mac Mini right now, you could receive it after the newer model has been announced. That's how far behind Apple has become in meeting demand.

The fastest way to get a Mac Mini right now is through Amazon. While configuration options are limited, you can buy an M4 Mac Mini with 24 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage and have it shipped in just a few days. You'll be paying $1,570, which is $471 more than what the Apple Store is charging. You can also get the M4 Pro Mac Mini for $1,570, which is only $100 more than Apple's prices and delivers within a week and a half. These are really the only models I recommend buying at this point.

Even Higher Prices

Prices have increased across the board on all Macs. At the beginning of May, Apple quietly discontinued the starting configuration of the Mac Mini, which used to come with 256 GB of storage and cost $599. This meant the starting price for a Mac Mini immediately jumped to $799.

Skip ahead to the end of June, and the 256-GB configuration has been brought back for $100 more at $699 (while the 512-GB model is also now up $100 to $899), in line with the price increases made to MacBooks. But the Mac Studio is where things have become very expensive. The starting price of the M4 Max Mac Studio went up to $2,499, a $500 hike. The most powerful option, the M3 Ultra Mac Studio, went from $3,999 to $5,299. Not only are we still waiting months for these devices, but they now also cost up to 25 percent more.

When announced, these “unavoidable” price increases, as Apple called them, were blamed on the skyrocketing prices of components like memory and storage. Consumer memory prices started increasing rapidly through the end of 2025, and laptop manufacturers began warning investors of the shortage heading into 2026. Now, we're seeing the full picture of the effect on Apple's ability to keep prices down and meet demand.

Apple has reportedly been seeking alternative sources for memory components, such as previously blacklisted Chinese companies, but this is a long-term problem. Most industry forecasting says memory costs won't come down at least until 2030, and memory manufacturer SK Hynix recently stated that 2027 may end up being the “worst year” for the shortage. Buckle up.

entries.title: Apple Upgrade Isn’t the Best Way to Buy an iPhone
entries.summary: With Apple Upgrade, the company is making it easier to pay for its products in monthly installments. Critics call it the “financialization of the affordability crisis.”
entries.content:
Apple has spent more than a decade tending to its thriving walled garden of products. Outgoing CEO Tim Cook’s core legacy at the company was turning it into a subscription service, where devices and services sync and communicate seamlessly, locking customers in.

Apple Upgrade is the latest iteration of that vision. On Tuesday, Apple announced a new product leasing service that lets you rent products like a new iPhone, iPad, Mac, or Apple Watch. (The news was leaked a week early by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.)

Apple Upgrade is a partnership with the financial company Klarna, known for its buy-now, pay-later services. If you sign up, you can pay a monthly fee to get a brand-new device. After a year or 24 months, you can keep paying the monthly fee but swap the hardware for something new. If you want something sooner, there’s a fee to swap devices before the 12-month mark.

Monthly plans start at $18 for iPhones, $12 for Apple Watches, $25 for Macs, and $12 for iPads. iPhones come unlocked, meaning your device isn’t tethered to a carrier and will work internationally with no issues. The program also offers device trade-in, which can lower the monthly amount you pay for the lease. Apple will also offer 3 percent daily cash back if you pay the lease with an Apple Card.

Paying $18 per month for 24 months is $432—that's for the $599 iPhone 17e. But that’s not exactly a discount, because you don’t own the device. iPhones tend to hold their value well, so buying a phone outright and reselling it is a better option financially. The fine print of Apple Upgrade also requires you to return the device in the initial condition you got it, meaning the company could charge more for any wear and tear. (You can pay a little more per month to add AppleCare insurance to the plan.)

Apple Upgrade also means the end of the company’s iPhone upgrade plan, a similar system that let people pay installments to buy the latest iPhone models. If you’re still enrolled in the program, Apple says you don’t have to take any action, and payments will continue until the end of your 24-month term. If your plan allows you to get a new device, Apple says it will “make it easy to get it in a way that works for you.” Or, you can continue paying out the existing loan and keep the device. You can switch from the iPhone upgrade plan to Apple Upgrade through your Apple account.

Fundamentally, Apple Upgrade functions as yet another way to keep users loyal to its product ecosystem. It also limits what people can do with their devices once they have them, as they’ll need to return them to the company later. Kyle Wiens, CEO of the repair company iFixit, says this move incrementally erodes people’s ownership of their devices.

“Apple is using their huge cash advantage to turn us all into renters rather than owners,” Wiens wrote in a text to WIRED. “That will cost people both money and agency. They know how much these phones are worth after a year and are maximizing their profit.”

An Apple representative indicated to WIRED that the ongoing memory shortage did not inspire Apple Upgrade, though it arrives shortly after Apple raised prices on several of its products. As everything gets more expensive, renting could be seen as a way of easing those added costs—all while still being able to use the latest and greatest device.

This is part of an ongoing “financialization of the affordability crisis,” as Whitney Barkley-Denney, a deputy director at the nonprofit Center for Responsible Lending, puts it. It’s part of a larger pattern of people using lending services or buy-now, pay-later plans like Klarna, Affirm, and Afterpay to pay for basic goods. These kinds of payments may seem smaller at first, but they add up and snowball into bigger financial problems.

“We aren't making things more affordable by doing this; we're just pushing it off down the road,” Barkley-Denney says. “It's in everyone's best interest for us to create a society that functions at a place where people can do all of these things without having to resort to borrowing for it.”

If you’re looking for the better value on your devices, Wiens says the answer is already out there.

“The best deal will remain what it's always been: Buy refurbished, keep it as long as you can, fix it when it breaks,” Wiens says. “Sell it when you're done for as much money as you possibly can.”

entries.title: Best Ethernet Switches: Fast, Reliable, and Secure
entries.summary: If your router is short on ports, you can add more with one of the best Ethernet switches. These are my top picks from what I’ve tested.
entries.content:
Modern routers and mesh systems offer better performance than ever, but many of them have a limited supply of ports. The best Ethernet switches enable you to add several Ethernet ports so you can wire up your most important connections for maximum speed, efficiency, and security.

Whether you want to set up a wired backhaul for better Wi-Fi performance, plug in your TV to banish buffering, or hook up a local, subscription-free security camera system using Power over Ethernet (PoE), Ethernet switches can help you do it. I’ve tested several, and these are the brands I recommend.

You may also want to dip into my other home networking guides, including What Is Ethernet, How to Run Ethernet Cables Around Your Home, How to Buy a Router, Best Wi-Fi Routers, and Best Mesh Systems.

Netgear Ethernet Switches

I’ve used a few different Netgear switches over the years and found them to be very reliable and well made.

If you just need a few extra ports, this affordable unmanaged switch from Netgear is nice and straightforward. The compact metal case offers five Gigabit ports; it’s plug-and-play, and it’s completely fanless for silent operation. It comes with a power adapter, each port has a green LED to show when it’s in use, and you can wall-mount or tuck it away. (Mine has been hiding in a cable tidy box).

If you need more ports, this smart switch has eight auto-sensing Gigabit Ethernet ports, each supporting up to 1,000 Mbps. It's plug-and-play and has a silent, fanless design. There’s a web-based user interface if you want to dig into settings to configure virtual local area networks (VLANs), set up Quality of Service (QoS) to prioritize traffic, mirror ports, and more.

TP-Link Ethernet Switches

Folks on a budget should consider an Ethernet switch from TP-Link. These are the ones I’ve tried and can recommend.

As simple as you get, this plug-and-play switch is sturdy with a metal case, has a silent fanless design, and gives you eight Gigabit Ethernet ports. I’ve been using it for several months to hook up various security camera hubs, NAS devices, and a Sonos speaker, and it works perfectly.

If you want a more compact, stylish design, my colleague has been using the TP-Link 8 Port Gigabit Ethernet Network Switch (TL-SG1008D) ($25) for years and says it works well.

I got this switch to connect three Power over Ethernet (PoE) cameras recently. It also has eight Gigabit ports, but four of them are PoE ports capable of supplying power (up to 30 watts each, but 64 watts in total), as well as carrying data. It’s sturdy and silent with LEDs on the front and ports on the back, which makes it a little easier to keep tidy and see what’s working at a glance. It’s also sturdy and silent. But because it’s fanless, it can get warm.

Other Ethernet Switch Manufacturers

I’m planning to test more Ethernet switches in the coming months, but most folks will be well served by something affordable from Netgear or TP-Link. I'm highlighting Ethernet switches for the average home user here, but there are many faster and larger options on the market. Other popular brands worth considering include Cisco, Trendnet, Zyxel, and Ubiquiti. I would steer clear of unknown brands.

How Many Ports Do You Need?

You can get Ethernet switches in all kinds of sizes, from four ports up to 24 or more. It’s probably a good idea to get a switch with at least a couple of spare ports to give yourself some space to add more wired devices in future. Remember, though, that one of the ports will be required for the incoming internet connection from your router.

What Speed Do You Need?

Most Ethernet switches for home users are rated at a Gigabit, so each port is capped at 1 Gbps. They will also have a backplane limit. It’s unlikely you’ll run into this as you probably won’t be maxing out every port simultaneously, but an 8-port Gigabit switch with a 4-Gbps backplane will be limited to 500 Mbps per port if they’re all maxing out. In practice, it will be less because you never get maximum efficiency.

You will, of course, also be limited by your overall internet speed. If your internet connection is only a max of 2 Gbps (and everything is online and maxed out), it’s going to be 250 Mbps per port maximum. You will still get the benefits of higher-rated gear for transfers between devices on your network, as they won’t be limited by your internet connection speed.

Unmanaged or Managed Switches?

Unmanaged switches are simple plug-and-play devices that don’t require any configuration, while managed switches allow you to configure and monitor your network. Most folks looking to add wired connections to their home network can save money and hassle by opting for an unmanaged switch.

If you want to use your switch to prioritize traffic, limit bandwidth, or create virtual local area networks (VLANs) you might consider a managed switch. One common use case might be to isolate specific devices like security cameras. You can usually configure these by visiting the IP address in your web browser or using a console client.

You can also get so-called “smart switches,” which behave like unmanaged switches out of the box but can be configured to some degree. These are a middle ground between unmanaged and managed.

Do You Need PoE?

If you are connecting security cameras or access points that support Power over Ethernet, you need a switch that can deliver that power. PoE switches deliver power and data via a single cable. Make sure your switch has enough PoE ports (some switches have a mix of regular and PoE ports) and can handle your overall power requirements. There are different PoE standards capable of delivering a different power budget per port, but you also have to consider the overall power budget.

  • Type 1 (IEEE 802.3af or PoE) can send 15 watts
  • Type 2 (IEEE 802.3at or PoE+) can send 30 watts
  • Type 3 (IEEE 802.3bt or PoE++) can send 60 watts
  • Type 4 (IEEE 802.3bt or PoE++) can send 90 watts

All of them will lose some power between the switch and device. You also have to match capable Ethernet cables.

This affordable cable is fine for data up to 1 Gbps, and I don't think most folks need to spend more. But if you are hooking up PoE devices, you'll need cables that can handle the additional load.
